items.q: (A) The news about the flood were broadcast on every channel last night, (B) so most families in the valley (C) had time to move (D) to higher ground.
options: The news about the flood were broadcast
so most families in the valley
items.correction: The news about the flood was broadcast
items.explanation: News looks plural but is an uncountable singular noun, so it takes a singular verb: the news was broadcast.

items.q: My cousin wants to become (A) an engineer, so she (B) studies the physics (C) for two hours every evening (D) after finishing her other homework.
items.explanation: School subjects and uncountable nouns used in a general sense take no article: she studies physics, not the physics.

items.q: The documentary we watched (A) in class explained how (B) ancient Egyptians built pyramids (C) by the help of ramps and (D) thousands of workers.
options: by the help of ramps and
items.correction: with the help of ramps and
items.explanation: The fixed phrase is with the help of; by marks the agent in a passive (built by workers), not the means with help.

items.q: Although the hike up the mountain (A) was exhausting, the view from the top (B) made us forget (C) how tired we were, and everyone (D) felt incredible happy.
items.explanation: A word that modifies an adjective (happy) must be an adverb: incredibly happy. Incredible is an adjective.

items.q: (A) Between you and I, the new coach (B) seems far stricter (C) than the last one, (D) who never made us run laps.
options: who never made us run laps
items.explanation: After a preposition such as between, a pronoun takes the object form: between you and me.

items.q: Of all the planets in our solar system, Jupiter (A) is by far the largest, (B) while Mercury, (C) the most close to the Sun, (D) is the smallest.
options: the most close to the Sun
items.explanation: One-syllable adjectives form the superlative with -est: the closest, not the most close.

items.q: If the school bus (A) had left on time this morning, we (B) would not have missed the first lesson, (C) and the teacher (D) will not be so angry now.
options: had left on time this morning
would not have missed the first lesson
will not be so angry now
items.correction: would not be so angry now
items.explanation: A past condition with a present result is a mixed conditional: if + past perfect, then would + verb for the present result, never will.

items.q: When I phoned the shop, the assistant (A) told me that they (B) will deliver the new printer (C) the following day (D) if I paid online.
items.explanation: In reported speech after a past reporting verb (told), will shifts back to would.

items.q: The small café (A) which we had lunch (B) was opened by two sisters (C) who studied cooking (D) in France for several years.
items.explanation: The relative clause describes a place, and café is not the object of had lunch, so the pronoun must be where (or at which), not which.

items.q: My brother (A) enjoys very much playing chess online, (B) but our parents think he (C) should spend more time (D) outdoors with his friends.
options: enjoys very much playing chess online
items.correction: enjoys playing chess online very much
items.explanation: A verb and its object are not separated by an adverb in English: enjoys playing chess online very much, with very much at the end.

items.q: While we were exploring the old market, my sister (A) stopped every few metres (B) to do photos of the (C) colourful fruit (D) piled on the wooden stalls.
items.explanation: The verb that collocates with photo is take: you take a photo, you do not do one.

items.q: Although the pupils tried (A) their best, the rope (B) they had brought (C) was not enough long (D) to reach the bottom of the well.
options: to reach the bottom of the well
items.explanation: Enough comes after an adjective or adverb (long enough), although it comes before a noun (enough rope).

items.q: When the fire alarm (A) rang during the chemistry lesson, all the students (B) left the building calmly and (C) waited outside until the teacher (D) tells them to go back.
items.explanation: The whole story is set in the past (rang, left, waited), so the final verb must also be in the past simple: told.

items.q: (A) Because of the roads were icy, the school (B) decided to start lessons (C) an hour later (D) than usual.
options: Because of the roads were icy
items.explanation: Because introduces a clause (subject + verb); because of is followed only by a noun phrase (because of the icy roads).

items.q: (A) Although the museum was crowded, (B) but we still managed (C) to see the famous painting (D) before closing time.
items.explanation: Although and but both express contrast, and English uses only one of them in a sentence, never both together.

items.q: The experiment failed (A) because we had added (B) too much salt and (C) too few water, (D) so the crystals never formed.
items.explanation: Water is uncountable, so its quantifier is little, not few: too little water.

items.q: The new manager (A) has promised to (B) listen to every complaint, (C) but so far he (D) has done very little progress.
items.explanation: Progress collocates with make, not do: you make progress.

items.q: I (A) am knowing Mrs Hoa (B) since she became our class teacher (C) three years ago, and I (D) have never seen her lose her temper.
options: since she became our class teacher
have never seen her lose her temper
items.explanation: Know is a stative verb, so it is not used in the continuous, and an action continuing from the past (since) takes the present perfect: have known.

items.q: The old theatre (A) is being repaired at the moment, so the concert (B) will hold in the sports hall (C) instead, which (D) can seat about five hundred people.
options: is being repaired at the moment
will hold in the sports hall
can seat about five hundred people
items.correction: will be held in the sports hall
items.explanation: The concert does not do the holding; it is held by someone, so the verb must be passive: will be held.

items.q: Passengers travelling on the night train (A) are reminded that they (B) should keep their luggage close and (C) must to show their tickets (D) whenever the inspector asks.
options: should keep their luggage close and
items.explanation: Must is a modal verb and is followed by the bare infinitive, without to: must show.

items.q: Before choosing a university, you (A) should talk to (B) as many people as possible and (C) not be afraid (D) to ask for a few advice.
options: as many people as possible and
to ask for a few advice
items.explanation: Advice is uncountable, so it cannot take a few; use some advice or a little advice.

items.q: (A) An university in the north has developed (B) a small robot that (C) can plant rice seedlings (D) three times faster than a farmer.
options: three times faster than a farmer
items.explanation: The article depends on the first sound: university begins with a /j/ sound, like yes, so it takes a, not an.

items.q: Scientists (A) believe that the Earth's temperature (B) is rising steadily since 1900, (C) mainly because of the gases (D) released by factories and cars.
items.explanation: Since + a starting point marks an action continuing from the past until now, which needs the present perfect (continuous): has been rising.

items.q: One of the reasons (A) why so many young people (B) love this sport is that it (C) don't require expensive equipment, (D) just a ball and some space.
options: love this sport is that it
just a ball and some space
items.explanation: The subject of the clause is it (the sport), a third-person singular, so the verb must be doesn't require.

items.q: After the long journey, the children (A) had a quick dinner, (B) brushed their teeth and (C) went straight (D) to the bed without complaining.
items.explanation: In fixed expressions about the purpose of a place, no article is used: go to bed, go to school, go to hospital.

items.q: (A) If I would have more free time, I (B) would learn to play the guitar, (C) but my timetable this year (D) leaves me no spare evenings.
options: If I would have more free time
would learn to play the guitar
items.correction: If I had more free time
items.explanation: In a second conditional the if-clause takes the past simple (if I had); would belongs only in the main clause.

items.q: The new smartphone (A) is very similar (B) with the old model, (C) except that its battery (D) lasts almost twice as long.
items.explanation: The adjective similar is followed by the preposition to: similar to, not similar with.

items.q: The city council (A) has decided to (B) replace the old buses with (C) electricity ones (D) to reduce air pollution in the centre.
options: to reduce air pollution in the centre
items.explanation: A noun (ones) is described by an adjective, so the form needed is electric; electricity is a noun.

items.q: In my opinion, badminton is (A) less tiring than football, (B) but it requires (C) quicker reactions, (D) so it is the most hardest sport to master.
options: so it is the most hardest sport to master
items.correction: so it is the hardest sport to master
items.explanation: Hard forms its superlative with -est: the hardest. Adding most as well makes a double superlative.

items.q: Most of my friends thought (A) this year's maths test was (B) more easier than last year's, (C) although the final question (D) took me nearly twenty minutes.
items.explanation: A short adjective forms its comparative with -er alone: easier. Adding more as well makes a double comparative.
